module_title: Cyber Law & Data Protection: Foundational Concepts
introduction: This foundational level explores the dual pillars of India's digital legal framework: The Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000 (which governs electronic commerce and cybercrimes), and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA), 2023 (which governs privacy and data usage).

core_concepts.title: The Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000
core_concepts.description:
The IT Act is India's primary law dealing with cybercrime and electronic commerce.
- Objective: To provide legal recognition for transactions carried out by means of electronic data interchange (e-commerce) and to grant legal recognition to Electronic Signatures.
- Jurisdiction: It applies to any offense or contravention committed outside India by any person (irrespective of nationality) if the act involves a computer, computer system, or network located inside India (Section 75).

core_concepts.title: The Shift to DPDPA, 2023
core_concepts.description: Historically, data protection in India was weakly governed by Section 43A of the IT Act. Following the landmark *Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)* judgment—which declared Privacy a Fundamental Right under Article 21—India drafted a dedicated privacy law. The DPDPA was passed in August 2023 to establish a comprehensive framework for processing digital personal data.

core_concepts.title: Core Entities under DPDPA
core_concepts.description:
The Act categorizes the digital ecosystem into specific roles:
1. Data Principal: The individual to whom the personal data relates (i.e., you, the citizen). For children, this includes parents/guardians.
2. Data Fiduciary: Any entity (company, government) that determines the *purpose and means* of processing personal data.
3. Data Processor: Any entity that processes personal data *on behalf of* a Data Fiduciary.

core_concepts.title: The 7 Core Principles of Data Protection
core_concepts.description:
The DPDPA is guided by a 'SARAL' (Simple, Accessible, Rational, Actionable) approach based on 7 global principles:
(1) Consent and Transparency, (2) Purpose Limitation (use data only for the stated reason), (3) Data Minimization (collect only what is necessary), (4) Accuracy, (5) Storage Limitation (delete it when done), (6) Security Safeguards, and (7) Accountability.

important_entities.name: Data Protection Board of India (DPBI)
important_entities.key_fact: The apex digital watchdog created by the DPDPA.
important_entities.significance: The DPBI is an independent body that oversees compliance, inquires into data breaches, and imposes massive financial penalties on non-compliant Data Fiduciaries. It officially began institutional operations in late 2025.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners often state: 'Under the DPDPA, personal data can NEVER be processed without the explicit consent of the Data Principal.' **FALSE**. The Act explicitly allows processing without consent for 'Certain Legitimate Uses', such as medical emergencies, disasters, state subsidies, or compliance with court judgments.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Principal = Person, Fiduciary = Founder of Purpose, Processor = Pawn
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use this to instantly remember who owns the data (Principal), who decides how to use it (Fiduciary), and who merely does the backend work (Processor).

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a Judiciary question asks 'Which landmark judgment necessitated the creation of the DPDPA, 2023?', unconditionally select **Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India** [1.2.2].
